o: Alice removes 10 stones, then each player removes one fewer than the opponent just removed; whoever cannot move loses. For n = 12, Alice takes 10 leaving 2, Bob cannot take 9, so Alice wins. For n = 1 Alice cannot even start and loses. With n ≤ 50 the removal amounts 10, 9, 8, ... terminate within ten steps, so direct simulation is simplest; a closed-form using the arithmetic-series partial sums also works.
k: The game lasts at most 10 moves (removals drop to 0 quickly), so simulation is trivially fast; the last player able to move wins.

a.i: Repeatedly subtract the current required amount (starting at 10, decrementing each turn) while the pile is large enough, toggling whose turn it is. When the loop stops, the player to move cannot move and loses, so Alice wins exactly when it is Bob's turn at that moment.
s: While n >= take: subtract take, decrement take, flip the turn.
Return true iff it is Bob's turn when the loop exits.
a.t: O(1) — at most 10 loop iterations regardless of n.

a.n: Approach 2: Closed Form via Partial Sums
a.i: After m successful moves the pile lost (10 + 9 + ... + (10-m+1)) = m(21-m)/2 stones. The total number of moves is the largest m with m(21-m)/2 <= n; Alice wins iff m is odd. Solve the quadratic m^2 - 21m + 2n >= 0 to get m = floor((21 - sqrt(441 - 8n)) / 2).
a.t: O(1) — one square root and a couple of corrections.

w: Simulation is the interview-safe choice — constant time anyway and impossible to get algebraically wrong. Pitfalls: returning the wrong polarity (whoever faces an unmovable requirement loses), and floating-point error in the closed form (fix with integer sqrt or adjust loops). Edge cases: n < 10 (Alice immediately loses), and exact boundary piles where the last legal move empties the pile. Follow-up: generalize the starting removal to k, or ask who wins under optimal play when players may remove any amount up to the current cap.
